```{python}
    go_to(p, "X", (15.0, -13.0), "route"); go_to(p, "Z", (15.0, 13.0), "route")
    p.dropback(1.5)
    for k_ in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k_, pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
    p.block("RB", pts=[(0.6, 1.0)])
    p.man("LCB", "X"); p.man("RCB", "Z")
    go_to(p, "FS", (15.0, 0.0), "drop", speed=1.5)
    for k_ in ("LDE", "LDT", "RDT", "RDE"):
        p.rush(k_, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (0.4, 2.4), "path", speed=3.0)     # right B gap (the tackle has the right A gap)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (0.6, -0.8), "path", speed=3.0)    # left A gap
    if not second_half:
        # man: each chaser trails his crosser by a step or two, on his hip, and loses ground in the traffic
        go_to(p, "NB", (4.9, 3.6), "path", via=[(4.6, -5.6), (4.5, -1.4)], speed=4.5)
        go_to(p, "SS", (6.3, -3.4), "path", via=[(6.2, 5.6), (6.3, 1.6)], speed=4.4)
        p.pass_to("H", t=1.75)
    else:
        # banjo: each sits in his area and takes whichever crosser comes to him
        go_to(p, "NB", (6.3, -6.6), "path", speed=2.4)
        go_to(p, "SS", (4.9, 6.6), "path", speed=2.4)
    return p


LAT, WIN = (-16.0, 16.0), (-7.8, 18.2)
T2 = 2.3
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.4, 5.9))
for row, sh in enumerate((False, True)):
    p = mesh(sh)
    df = tracking(p)
    rings = (("NB", PURPLE), ("SS", PURPLE)) if sh else ()
    for col, t in enumerate((0.0, T2)):
        ax = axes[row, col]
        f = panel(ax, p, df, t, LAT, WIN, rings=rings)
        half = "Second half" if sh else "First half"
        ax.set_title(f"{half}: " + ("snap" if t == 0 else f"+{t:.1f} s"), fontsize=8.4, color=style.INK, loc="left",
                     fontweight="bold")
        if col == 1:
            hd, hw = p.position("H", t)
            yd, yw = p.position("Y", t)
            if not sh:
                say(f, p, 12.0, -6.5, "man: each chaser\na step behind", fontsize=6.3, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
                say(f, p, hd + 3.0, hw + 2.6, "H open", fontsize=6.3, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
            else:
                point_to(f, p, (12.0, -8.5), (6.3, -6.6), "$ takes Y", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.3)
                point_to(f, p, (12.0, 9.0), (4.9, 6.6), "SS takes H", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.3)
                say(f, p, -5.6, 9.5, "nobody open", fontsize=6.3, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
        else:
            say(f, p, 10.0, -9.0, "same look\nboth halves", fontsize=6.3, color=style.INK_2)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.0, w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

The second-half picture in @fig-before-after looks like a win for the defense, and for a series or two it
is. But every fix gives something away, and this one does too: the two inside defenders now *stop* and
wait. What that hands the offense is the next call after the call, and you'll get to make it yourself in
the second drill at the end of the chapter.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: the same pair from real tracking data"}
With Big Data Bowl tracking data you can build @fig-before-after from real plays: find two snaps from
the same game, the same offense and a similar look, one from each half, and draw each at the snap and a
couple of seconds later. The online version of this chapter includes a short code sketch that does it
with `gridiron.bdb` (it isn't run here, because the tracking files are a separate download from Kaggle). The 2025 edition's files cover weeks 1–9
of the 2022 season, with pre-snap frames included ([Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd)).
:::

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (the real-data version: one play from each half of the same game)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, frame_strip

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")        # Big Data Bowl 2025 files (2022 season, weeks 1-9)
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
game = plays[plays["gameId"] == 2022091100]                       # pick a game
third = game[(game["down"] == 3) & (game["passResult"].notna())]
first_half = third[third["quarter"] <= 2].iloc[0]
second_half = third[third["quarter"] >= 3].iloc[0]
for row in (first_half, second_half):
    one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=row["gameId"], play_id=row["playId"])
    frame_strip(one, times=[0.0, 2.3], title=f"Q{row['quarter']}: {row['pff_passCoverage']}")
```

## Do halftime adjustments decide games? Testing the narrative

Back to the analyst's line. If halftime adjustments decide games, three things should show up in the data:
second halves should look different from first halves in a way that favors the team with the better
staff; a team's first-half performance shouldn't tell you much about its second half (the adjustment
breaks the pattern); and some coaches should be consistently better than others at turning a game around
after halftime. The play-by-play data lets us check each one. All the numbers below use regular-season
games from 2006 to 2025 and leave out the last two minutes of each half and snaps where one team's win
probability was above 90%, so that two-minute drills and garbage time don't dominate.[^halfdata]

**First: second halves look exactly like first halves, on average.** League-wide, offenses averaged
`{python} f"{LEAGUE_HALF['Half1']:+.3f}"` EPA per play in first halves and
`{python} f"{LEAGUE_HALF['Half2']:+.3f}"` in second halves. If defenses (or offenses) systematically
out-adjusted the other side at halftime, you'd expect a gap. There isn't one, which is what you'd expect if
both sides adjust about equally well, and if most adjusting happens every series rather than once.

**Second: the first half tells you very little about the second half, and that's mostly not adjustment.**
@fig-halftime-test (left) splits about `{python} f"{len(TG):,}"` team-games by how well each offense played in
the first half. Offenses that were terrible before halftime were much better after it, and offenses that
were brilliant came back to earth. The correlation between a team's first-half and second-half EPA per
play in the same game is only `{python} f"{R_HALVES:.2f}"`.

That looks like a story about adjustments, and it's the classic trap of
*regression to the mean*. A first half is about 25 to 35 snaps, and EPA per play over that few snaps is
mostly noise: a fumble, a dropped pass, a 60-yard run. An offense that had an awful first half was
usually an ordinary offense having an unlucky half, and its next half looks ordinary, *whether or not
anyone adjusted anything*. The team that "came out a different team after halftime" was often just the
same team without the bad bounces. The same arithmetic makes the hot first-half team cool off.

```{python}
#| label: fig-halftime-test
#| fig-cap: "Testing the halftime narrative, 2006–2025 regular seasons (neutral snaps). Left: team-games grouped into tenths by the offense's first-half EPA per play; each dot is a group's average first half (x) against its second half (y). If the first half carried over, the dots would lie on the dashed diagonal; instead they lie almost flat: bad first halves were followed by about average second halves, and great ones too. That is regression to the mean, not proof of adjustment. Right: is 'improving after halftime' a team trait? Each dot is a team-season's second-half minus first-half EPA per play, plotted against the same team's number the next season. There is essentially no relationship (r near zero), while a team's overall EPA per play carries over from one season to the next quite strongly (r about 0.4). Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
ax = axes[0]
lim = (-0.62, 0.55)
ax.plot(lim, lim, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, zorder=1)
ax.plot(DEC["h1"], DEC["h2"], color=style.SERIES[0], lw=1.2, zorder=2)
ax.scatter(DEC["h1"], DEC["h2"], s=26, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=3)
ax.set_xlim(*lim); ax.set_ylim(*lim)
ax.set_xlabel("First-half EPA per play", fontsize=7.8)
ax.set_ylabel("Second-half EPA per play", fontsize=7.8)
ax.set_title("A bad first half, then an average second", fontsize=8.4)
ax.text(0.12, 0.33, "if the first half\ncarried over", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="center")
ax.annotate("worst tenth of\nfirst halves", (DEC["h1"].iloc[0], DEC["h2"].iloc[0]), xytext=(-0.42, 0.24),
            fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK, ha="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.7))
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
ax = axes[1]
ax.scatter(PO["diff"], PO["diff_next"], s=9, color=style.SERIES[0], alpha=0.45, lw=0, zorder=2)
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, zorder=1); ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8, zorder=1)
ax.set_xlim(-0.32, 0.32); ax.set_ylim(-0.32, 0.32)
ax.set_xlabel("2nd-half minus 1st-half EPA/play, season N", fontsize=7.8)
ax.set_ylabel("Same, season N+1", fontsize=7.8)
ax.set_title("'Second-half team' is not a trait", fontsize=8.4)
ax.text(0.30, -0.24, f"r = {R_DIFF_O:.2f}\n(overall EPA/play: r = {R_ALL_O:.2f})", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK,
        ha="right", va="center", bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.4)
plt.show()
```

**Third: no team or coach is reliably a "second-half team."** The right panel of @fig-halftime-test asks
whether improving after halftime is a repeatable trait. If some staffs adjusted better than others, a team
that improved after halftime in one season should tend to do it again the next. It doesn't: the
year-to-year correlation of a team's second-half-minus-first-half EPA per play is
`{python} f"{R_DIFF_O:.2f}"` for offenses and `{python} f"{R_DIFF_D:.2f}"` for defenses, against
`{python} f"{R_ALL_O:.2f}"` and `{python} f"{R_ALL_D:.2f}"` for how good the offense and defense are
overall. Being good carries over from one season to the next; being better after halftime doesn't.

Coaches are the natural place to look next, since a reputation for halftime magic attaches to a person.
@fig-coach-halves plots every head coach with at least 100 games in these seasons by his teams' average
scoring margin in first halves and in second halves.

```{python}
#| label: fig-coach-halves
#| fig-cap: "Head coaches with at least 100 regular-season games, 2006–2025: average scoring margin per game in first halves (x) and in second halves, regulation only (y). The dashed diagonal is 'just as good after halftime as before.' Good coaches are good in both halves, so the dots rise from left to right. A 'halftime adjuster' would sit well above the diagonal; nobody does by more than about two and a half points a game, and nearly every coach's gap is within two standard errors of zero, about what chance alone produces over 100 to 300 games. The two coaches with the best reputations as game planners, Bill Belichick and Andy Reid, sit *below* it: their teams were better before halftime, and they often led at the half. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.6))
lim = (-3.6, 5.2)
ax.plot(lim, lim, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.7, zorder=1); ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.7, zorder=1)
ax.scatter(COACH["h1"], COACH["h2"], s=COACH["n"] / 6, color=style.SERIES[0], alpha=0.75, lw=0, zorder=3)
label_at = {"Bill Belichick": (-0.5, 0.55), "Andy Reid": (0.25, -0.55), "Sean Payton": (-1.2, 0.55),
            "Pete Carroll": (-1.5, 0.35), "Mike Tomlin": (-0.2, -0.75), "John Harbaugh": (0.3, 0.45),
            "Sean McDermott": (-0.4, 0.62), "Kyle Shanahan": (0.4, -0.6), "Kevin Stefanski": (0.3, -0.45),
            "Mike Shanahan": (-1.1, -0.45)}
for nm, (dx, dy) in label_at.items():
    if nm in COACH.index:
        x, y = COACH.loc[nm, "h1"], COACH.loc[nm, "h2"]
        ax.annotate(nm, (x, y), xytext=(x + dx, y + dy), fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK, ha="center", va="center",
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.6, shrinkA=1, shrinkB=3))
ax.text(5.0, -3.0, "dashed line: as good after\nhalftime as before", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="right", va="bottom")
ax.set_xlim(*lim); ax.set_ylim(-3.2, 4.8)
ax.set_xlabel("First-half scoring margin per game", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Second-half scoring margin per game", fontsize=8)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
plt.show()
```

Two forces you can see in @fig-coach-halves explain most of what fans read as halftime magic.

- **Score effects.** Teams that lead at halftime play differently afterwards: they run more, take fewer risks
  and drain the clock, while teams that trail throw more and gamble. Across these seasons, teams leading by
  1 to 13 points at the half were outscored by about
  `{python} f"{-LEAD_BINS.iloc[3]['mean']:.1f}"` points in the second half on average, and teams trailing by
  1 to 13 outscored their opponents by the mirror amount. That pushes every good team's second-half
  margin down and every trailing team's up, with no locker-room speech required.
- **Possessions.** One team gets the ball first in the second half, and sometimes a long first-half drive
  means one offense barely played. Second halves can look like turnarounds simply because one offense
  finally got the ball.

None of this means adjustments are fake. Coaches adjust constantly; the between-series loop is real work
that wins plays. The data says something narrower: adjustment is not a *halftime* event that reliably
separates staffs, and a big second-half swing is usually explained by noise, score and possessions before
you need to credit genius. When a team does turn a game around, look for the specific change.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sb57
#| fig-cap: "Super Bowl LVII by half (runs and passes only). Kansas City's offense ran only 20 plays before halftime to Philadelphia's 44; its EPA per play rose from about +0.15 to about +0.5 (small samples) and its rushing yards from 36 to 126, while its motion rate barely moved. More snaps, a run game and two well-timed calls, not a new motion offense. Sources: nflverse play-by-play; FTN charting (`is_motion`)."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(6.6, 2.05))
H = ["Half1", "Half2"]
xl = ["1st", "2nd"]
ax = axes[0]
w = 0.38
for i, (tm, c) in enumerate((("KC", style.SERIES[0]), ("PHI", style.SERIES[1]))):
    vals = [SB.loc[(tm, hh), "snaps"] for hh in H]
    ax.bar(np.arange(2) + (i - 0.5) * w, vals, width=w, color=c, label=tm, zorder=3)
    for j, v in enumerate(vals):
        ax.text(j + (i - 0.5) * w, v + 1, f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK)
ax.set_title("Offensive snaps", fontsize=7.8); ax.set_ylim(0, 58)
ax.legend(fontsize=6.2, loc="upper right", handlelength=1.0, borderaxespad=0.2)
for ax, col, ttl, fmt, ylim in ((axes[1], "epa", "KC: EPA per play", "{:+.2f}", (0, 0.7)),
                                (axes[2], "rush_yds", "KC: rushing yards", "{:.0f}", (0, 150)),
                                (axes[3], "motion", "KC: motion rate", "{:.0%}", (0, 0.7))):
    vals = [SB.loc[("KC", hh), col] for hh in H]
    ax.bar(np.arange(2), vals, width=0.55, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=3)
    for j, v in enumerate(vals):
        ax.text(j, v + ylim[1] * 0.02, fmt.format(v), ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK)
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=7.8); ax.set_ylim(*ylim)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xticks(range(2), xl, fontsize=6.8); ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=6.2)
    ax.set_xlabel("half", fontsize=6.6)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
axes[3].yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.9)
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Kansas City Chiefs, Super Bowl LVII (2022 season)"}
Super Bowl LVII (February 12, 2023) is everyone's favorite example of a halftime turnaround. The Eagles
led 24–14 at the half; Patrick Mahomes had re-aggravated his injured ankle late in the second quarter; and
the Chiefs scored on all four of their second-half possessions to win 38–35, including two fourth-quarter
touchdowns on the same motion play (the story of "Corn Dog" is told in
[Motion and Shifts](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd) and
[What Beats What](08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd)).[^sb57] "Kansas City's halftime adjustments" is the
usual summary. What does the data say changed?


**What to notice:** start with the first panel of @fig-sb57. Kansas City's offense barely played in the first half:
`{python} f"{SB.loc[('KC', 'Half1'), 'snaps']:.0f}"` runs and passes against Philadelphia's
`{python} f"{SB.loc[('PHI', 'Half1'), 'snaps']:.0f}"`, because the Eagles' offense held the ball for long
drives. The Chiefs had been effective when they did have it, about
`{python} f"{SB.loc[('KC', 'Half1'), 'epa']:+.2f}"` EPA per play, and the second half gave them
`{python} f"{SB.loc[('KC', 'Half2'), 'snaps']:.0f}"` snaps. Some of the change was real and visible: the
run game went from `{python} f"{SB.loc[('KC', 'Half1'), 'rush_yds']:.0f}"` rushing yards to
`{python} f"{SB.loc[('KC', 'Half2'), 'rush_yds']:.0f}"`, with Isiah Pacheco and Jerick McKinnon running
well and Mahomes scrambling on the bad ankle. What *didn't*
change much was the motion: by FTN's charting the Chiefs used motion on
`{python} pct(SB.loc[('KC', 'Half1'), 'motion'])` of first-half snaps and
`{python} pct(SB.loc[('KC', 'Half2'), 'motion'])` after halftime.[^ftn] The two motion touchdowns were a
game-plan call used at the right moment near the goal line (the second one set up by Kadarius Toney's
65-yard punt return, the longest in Super Bowl history), not a new offense invented in the locker room.

So was it halftime adjustments? Partly: the Chiefs ran more and ran better, and the staff saved its best
red-zone call for the moments that mattered. But the honest summary also includes more possessions, a punt
return and a defense that had played a lot of snaps. That's the habit this chapter wants you to build:
when someone credits halftime, ask what changed, and check how much of it was the clock and the bounces.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: the adjustment hunter"}
Pick one team for a game and keep a short list in two columns, first half and second half.

**Before the snap**

- **Personnel:** which groups does the offense use, and does the defense still match them? A team that
  lived in 11 personnel and comes out in 12 has changed its plan.
- **Tempo:** does the offense go fast after big plays? Does the defense look rushed, with players running
  off at the snap or a plain, undisguised look?
- **Motion:** more or less of it after halftime, and does the defense still follow it the same way?
- **Coverage shell:** two-high or one-high before the snap, and does it change after the half?

**After the snap**

- **Pressure:** count rushers on third down in each half. Did a blitz that worked disappear, or one that
  got burned stop coming?
- **Protection:** is a back or tight end staying in to help a struggling tackle after halftime?
- **The fix and the answer:** when the defense changes something, watch the next series. Does the offense
  call the play that beats the change? That's the call after the call.

Then check the box score: who had more snaps in each half, and who led at halftime? Before you credit an
adjustment, ask whether the scoreboard and the clock explain the second half.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the same eleven, in a hurry"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-freeze
#| fig-cap: "First-and-10, second quarter. On the previous snap the offense, in 12 personnel with both tight ends attached, gained 19 yards on a play-action pass; the defense was in base personnel. Eight seconds after the tackle the offense is set again with the same eleven players, both tight ends flexed into the slots. The defensive coordinator waved for his nickel back, then waved him off. The defense's outside linebackers have stayed close to the box (purple rings) and the safeties are deep."
p = Play(flexed_12(), base_vs_flexed(False), los=50, to_go=10)
p.highlight("SAM", "WILL", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-8.6, 15.5), width_in=5.6)
point_to(f, p, (9.0, -10.6), (-1.5, -8.0), "U: nobody within\n6 yards", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (9.0, 10.8), (-1.5, 8.0), "Y: nobody within\n6 yards", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
say(f, p, -7.4, 10.0, "same 11 as last snap,\nno huddle", fontsize=6.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

**What will the offense do, and when will it snap?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Snap fast and throw quickly to a tight end, most likely Y or U on a quick hitch, out or seam, before the
linebackers can widen.** This is the substitution freeze working exactly as designed. The defense is stuck in
base personnel, and its outside linebackers have chosen to stay near the box, where they're useful against
the run. That leaves both flexed tight ends with soft or no coverage underneath: the nearest defenders are a
linebacker several yards inside and a safety eleven yards deep. A tempo offense's quarterback is usually
taught a simple count rule for this: if they won't cover him, throw it to him.

If instead the linebackers had walked out over the tight ends (as in @fig-freeze), the count flips: five
defenders in the box against five linemen, and the offense would run the ball, or throw at the linebacker
covering a tight end in space. Either way the offense wants the snap *now*, before the defense can get a
call in or call a timeout. The defense's best realistic answer, if it sees this coming, is a timeout to get
its nickel on the field, which costs it a timeout in the first half: exactly the trade tempo is designed to
force.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the call after the call"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-sit
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-6, third quarter. Same offense, same 2x2 formation as in the first half, when mesh (two shallow crossers) beat the defense's man coverage three times. Since halftime the defense has shown the same single-high look, but its two inside defenders (purple rings) now sit at five yards and pass the crossers off to each other, and it has stopped three straight crossing plays. The faint dashed arrows show what those two defenders did on those plays: they stepped up and sat."
p = Play(spread(), cover1_look(), los=62, to_go=6)
p.highlight("NB", "SS", color=PURPLE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-16.5, 16.5), window=(-8.6, 15.5), width_in=5.6)
ghost(f, p, [(5.5, -7.8), (4.8, -4.0)], alpha=0.85, lw=1.6)
ghost(f, p, [(6.0, 7.8), (4.0, 4.6)], alpha=0.85, lw=1.6)
point_to(f, p, (10.6, -2.0), (4.6, -4.2), "since halftime:\nstep up and sit", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
plt.show()
```

**The offense has seen the adjustment. What does it call now, and who is it aimed at?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A route that uses the sitting defenders' new habit against them: most likely a pivot (whip) route by a slot
receiver, or a crosser that keeps climbing behind them, with the target being the space the sitter just
committed to leave.** The second-half rule tells each inside defender to stop at about five yards and take
whoever comes into his area. A slot receiver who runs straight at that defender as if he's crossing, then
plants and snaps back the way he came, is working against a man who has just committed to the cross; the
defender is standing still and has to turn and chase. Many offenses pair it with a crosser from the other
side that, instead of flattening at five yards, keeps climbing to eight or ten, behind the sitters and in
front of the deep safety.

This is the call after the call: the offense isn't trying to beat the first-half man coverage any more,
and it isn't simply running mesh again. It's punishing the specific way the defense fixed mesh. Expect the
defense to answer that, too, perhaps by mixing the man coverage back in so the sitters can't be read in
advance. If you said "run the ball," that's reasonable partial credit: two defenders standing at five yards
looking for crossers are a step slower to the run, but on third-and-6 most play-callers would rather attack
the adjustment directly.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: the quick huddle on fourth down"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-sugar
#| fig-cap: "Fourth-and-1 near midfield, early in the fourth quarter. On third down the offense was stopped a yard short. Instead of waiting, it has gathered in a tight huddle about five yards behind the ball, already with three tight ends and a fullback on the field, while the defense still has its base personnel out there and its heavier short-yardage group waiting on the sideline. The play clock shows 35."
huddle = []
names = [("QB", "QB", "Q"), ("C", "C", "C"), ("LG", "LG", ""), ("RG", "RG", ""), ("LT", "LT", ""), ("RT", "RT", ""),
         ("RB", "RB", "R"), ("FB", "FB", "F"), ("Y", "TE", "Y"), ("U", "TE", "U"), ("W", "TE", "W")]
for i, (k_, pos_, lab) in enumerate(names):
    a = 2 * np.pi * i / len(names)
    huddle.append(O(k_, pos_, -7.0 + 3.0 * np.cos(a), 3.3 * np.sin(a), lab))
p = Play(huddle, base_vs_tight(), los=58, to_go=1)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-15.0, 15.0), window=(-12.0, 15.5), width_in=5.4)
say(f, p, -7.0, 8.8, "quick huddle\n4–5 yards back", fontsize=6.6, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK)
say(f, p, 11.5, 7.0, "base defense still on;\nshort-yardage group\non the sideline", fontsize=6.4, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
plt.show()
```

**Why huddle so close, and what's likely to happen in the next ten seconds?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**It's a sugar huddle, and the offense wants to snap before the defense can get its short-yardage personnel
on the field, set its own call, or call a timeout: expect a fast snap and a short-yardage run, most likely
a quarterback sneak or an inside run behind the extra tight ends.** The huddle lets the offense give a precise
call to everyone at once (no signals for the defense to steal) and still get to the line almost
immediately. Because the offense already has its heavy personnel on the field from third down and isn't
substituting now, the umpire won't stand over the ball for the defense: if the defense starts sending in
its goal-line players, it risks being caught with twelve on the field.

The defense's realistic choices are to play the down with what it has, using a simple short-yardage
call, or to spend a timeout, which buys it a substitution and a call but costs it a timeout in the fourth
quarter and gives the offense time to think about a different play. Some offenses also use the threat
itself: a quick huddle that makes the defense burn a timeout has already won something.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Adjusting is constant and small.** Between series, the booth's tallies and the tablet photos meet the
  coaches and players on the bench, and what comes out is a rule, an alignment, a protection call or a
  re-ranked call sheet, chosen from plays already practiced.
- **Tempo is a weapon about the rules, not just speed.** The defense may match personnel only when the
  offense substitutes, so an offense that keeps its eleven and goes fast freezes the defense in the wrong
  players, tires it, and strips away its disguise. The sugar huddle gets the same benefits with a huddle's
  clarity.
- **Tempo costs the offense too.** One personnel group, simple calls, tired players and, above all, its own
  defense back on the field after a fast three-and-out. Kelly's Eagles were the fastest offense in the
  league for three seasons and their defense faced the most plays each year.
- **Defenses answer tempo by being sound rather than clever:** one-word calls, rules the players finish
  themselves, and versatile players who never need to come off. The league polices the rest.
- **The call after the call** is choosing the play that beats the defense's *next* answer. Watch the series
  after a team fixes something.
- **"Halftime adjustments" mostly don't survive the data as a decisive, repeatable skill.** First and second
  halves look the same league-wide, bad halves regress to the mean, being better after halftime doesn't carry
  over from season to season, and score effects and possessions explain most big swings. Ask what changed.

    <https://operations.nfl.com/the-game/technology/sideline-of-the-future/>. What each staff puts in its booth, and who
    sits there, varies by team.

[^surface]: NFL Football Operations, "Sideline Technology": "Starting in the 2014 season, all teams have sideline access
    to league-provided, specially configured Microsoft Surface tablets, on which they receive high-resolution color
    images almost instantaneously": <https://operations.nfl.com/the-game/technology/sideline-of-the-future/>. The league
    tested video on the tablets in the 2015 preseason; regular-season use has been limited to still images. See
    NFL.com, "Surface tablets might have found permanent home on NFL sideline":
    <https://www.nfl.com/news/surface-tablets-might-have-found-permanent-home-on-nfl-sideline-0ap3000000430360>.
    Proposals to add video were made but not adopted; when college football first allowed in-game video on its sideline
    tablets in 2024, the NFL still allowed only still images (Sportico, Aug. 2024:
    <https://www.sportico.com/leagues/college-sports/2024/college-football-sideline-tablet-video-rules-2024-1234793971>),
    and the league's own page, updated for the 2025 switch to Surface Copilot+ PCs, still describes images only.

[^equity]: NFL Football Operations, "NFL Equity Rule," which limits each club to as many working sideline and booth
    viewing devices as its opponent has: <https://operations.nfl.com/gameday/behind-the-scenes/nfl-equity-rule>.

[^halftime]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 4, Section 1, Article 3: "Between the second and third periods, there shall be an
    intermission of 13 minutes": <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>. Super Bowl halftimes run longer
    for the show.

[^playclock]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 4, Section 6, Article 1 (the 40-second play clock, which starts when a play ends)
    and Article 2 (a 25-second clock after certain administrative stoppages):
    <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>.

[^tempodata]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play (`game_seconds_remaining`), regular seasons. A pair of
    snaps counts when both are runs or passes on the same drive and quarter, nothing else is logged between them, the
    earlier play was a run or a completed pass that did not go out of bounds and had no penalty, timeout, touchdown,
    lost fumble or spike, both snaps came with win probability between 20% and 80%, and the earlier snap came with more
    than 2:30 left in the half (so the two-minute warning and the late-half out-of-bounds clock rules can't interfere).
    Gaps under 5 or over 60 seconds are dropped as clock errors. The number includes the duration of the earlier play
    (usually 4–7 seconds), so it is not the same as time left on the play clock; nflverse's `play_clock` field is not
    usable for this. The 30-second threshold is this chapter's choice.

[^subrule]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 5, Section 2, Article 10 ("If a substitution is made by the offense before the
    two-minute warning of either half, the offense shall not be permitted to snap the ball until the defense has been
    permitted to respond with its substitutions"; "The Umpire will stand over the ball until the Referee deems that the
    defense has had a reasonable time to complete its substitutions"; a first violation brings a warning and a replay of
    the down, later ones a 15-yard unsportsmanlike conduct foul) and Article 11 (simulated substitutions):
    <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>. On too many men, Rule 5, Section 1, and
    [What a Play Really Is](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd).

[^zebras25]: Football Zebras, "NFL officials instructed on new procedures for substitution tactics" (Oct. 2, 2025): defenses
    that substitute "at less than normal speed" have the window closed; a simulated substitution opens a substitution
    period, with a warning and then a 15-yard unsportsmanlike conduct foul if the offense snaps during it; field goals
    and the last two minutes are exempt; prompted by a Green Bay simulated substitution in Week 3:
    <https://www.footballzebras.com/2025/10/nfl-officials-instructed-on-new-procedures-for-substitution-tactics/>.

[^sugarlions]: Kirsten Tanis, "One big change coming to the Chicago Bears' new offense," *Sports Illustrated* Bear Digest
    (July 10, 2025), on Johnson's use of "sugar huddles, where the normal huddle takes place but then is broken rapidly

    <https://www.prideofdetroit.com/2024/12/10/24317435/detroit-lions-film-breakdown-all-22-green-bay-packers-fourth-down-attempts-thursday-night-football>.

    history for most ball control plays from scrimmage with 1,199 in 1994, 1,191 in 2012 and 1,187 in 1995":
    <https://www.patriots.com/news/inside-the-numbers-regular-season-recap-194956>. In this course's tempo measure
    (the twenty-season chart) the 2012 Patriots were the league's fastest team.

[^kellybio]: "Chip Kelly," Wikipedia (Oregon head coach 2009–2012; Eagles 2013–2015; 49ers 2016):
    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chip_Kelly>.

[^kellyexit]: The Eagles released DeSean Jackson on March 28, 2014 (ESPN, "Eagles release DeSean Jackson": <https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/10688873>),

    Kelly on Dec. 29, 2015, with one game left and the team 6–9 (PhillyVoice:
    <https://phillyvoice.com/philadelphia-eagles-release-head-coach-chip-kelly>).

[^moore]: The Saints hired Moore, the Eagles' offensive coordinator, as head coach on Feb. 11, 2025 (ESPN:
    <https://africa.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/43630181/new-orleans-saints-hiring-kellen-moore-philadelphia-eagles-super-bowl-2025>).

[^phi13]: Pro Football Reference, 2013 Philadelphia Eagles (10–6, first in the NFC East; LeSean McCoy led the league in
    rushing): <https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/phi/2013.htm>. In this course's nflverse count the Eagles also
    led all teams in rushing yards that season.

[^kellydata]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 2013–2015, runs and passes (scrambles and
    sacks counted as passes; two-point tries excluded). Offensive rank is by EPA per play among 32 teams. Tempo numbers
    use the method in the note on the tempo chart.

[^giants11]: Associated Press, "NFL memo warns teams on faking injuries" (Sept. 21, 2011), after Deon Grant and Jacquian
    Williams went down against the Rams' no-huddle; the memo warned of "fines, suspensions and loss of draft picks":
    <https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2011/sep/21/nfl-memo-warns-teams-on-faking-injuries/>. Grant denied faking.

[^injury]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 4, Section 5, Article 3 (injury timeouts before the two-minute warning: "the
    injured player must leave the game for the completion of one down," with exceptions):
    <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>.

[^ncaa10]: *Sports Illustrated*, "NCAA proposes rule change to allow time for defensive substitutions" (Feb. 12, 2014),
    on the proposal that offenses could not snap until 29 seconds remained on the play clock, outside the last two
    minutes of each half: <https://www.si.com/college/2014/02/12/ncaa-rule-change-defensive-substitutions-targeting>.
    The rules committee tabled it on March 5, 2014, before the Playing Rules Oversight Panel could vote on it: Associated
    Press, "NCAA tables 10-second football rule proposal," *Bangor Daily News* (March 5, 2014):
    <https://www.bangordailynews.com/2014/03/05/sports/ncaa-tables-10-second-football-rule-proposal/>.

[^halfdata]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, regular seasons 2006–2025. Snaps are runs and passes with a
    down recorded, more than two minutes left in the half and win probability between 10% and 90%. A team-game is kept if
    the offense had at least 15 such snaps in the first half and 10 in the second. Season-to-season correlations pair
    each team with itself the next season (608 pairs). The coach chart uses actual scores at the end of the second and
    fourth quarters (overtime excluded) and each game's listed head coach; coaches with at least 100 games in these
    seasons are shown. Under pure chance, the standard error of a coach's second-half-minus-first-half margin over a few
    hundred games is about 0.5–1 point, so differences of up to about 2 points are unremarkable.

[^sb57]: "Super Bowl LVII," Wikipedia (Kansas City 38, Philadelphia 35, Feb. 12, 2023; 24–14 Philadelphia at
    halftime): <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_LVII>; *Sports Illustrated*, "Patrick Mahomes Reinjures Ankle in
    Second Quarter of Super Bowl LVII" (Feb. 13, 2023):
    <https://www.si.com/nfl/2023/02/13/patrick-mahomes-reinjures-ankle-second-quarter-super-bowl-lvii>; Chiefs.com,
    "Kadarius Toney Comes Through in a Big Way as Part of Record-Setting Super Bowl" (65-yard punt return, the longest in

    Snap counts, EPA and rushing yards by half are a course calculation from nflverse play-by-play.

[^ftn]: FTN charting via nflverse (`load_ftn_charting`), whose `is_motion` flag means motion occurred on the play before
    *or at* the snap: <https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_ftn_charting.html>. It is not comparable with
    PFF's shift-and-motion series.
